newsitem.title: USA: CIA veterans honor partners in secret war in Laos.
newsitem.headline: CIA veterans honor partners in secret war in Laos.

text.p: Former CIA and U.S. military officers paid glowing tributes on Wednesday to the largely unsung "secret army" that fought for the United States in Laos during the Vietnam War.

But members of the anti-communist force, chiefly mountain-dwelling ethnic Hmong tribesmen, applauded loudest when members of Congress vowed to press their case for overcoming barriers to U.S. citizenship.

An estimated 3,000 Hmong and Lao veterans, most clad in U.S. Army camouflage fatigues, gathered beside the Vietnam Veterans Memorial for what organisers called long-overdue recognition of their contribution to the U.S. cause in Southeast Asia from 1961 to 1975.
"U.S. citizenship for our brothers!" shouted Representative Bruce Vento, a Democrat from Minnesota, home to more than 35,000 Hmong refugees, the largest concentration outside of Laos.

Vento is the author of a bill that would change the rules for Hmong naturalisation. It would waive the English-language competency test and the residency requirement for Hmong and Lao veterans who fought in the "secret war," the CIA's largest covert action.

After an awards ceremony, the veterans marched across the Potomac River to Arlington National Cemetery to symbolise their flight across the Mekong to Thailand after the communist victory in 1975. At the cemetery on Thursday, they were to unveil the first war memorial to their service.

The U.S. involvement in Laos had the same goal as in neighbouring Vietnam -- to keep pro-communist insurgents backed by North Vietnam at bay. But Laos, by agreement of the major powers at Geneva in 1962, was to remain neutral, and both sides pretended to honour that neutrality.

In his first public speech about the still-largely undocumented secret war, Theodore Shackley, the CIA station chief in Laos from 1966 to 1968, credited the secret army with battling North Vietnamese communist forces to a standstill in the north of Laos for 10 years.

At the time, North Vietnamese troops, together with their communist Pathet Lao allies, were pushing hard to enlarge and defend an elaborate logistical pipeline to the south, the so-called Ho Chi Minh Trail.

"In north Laos, the task was to fight a war of position and manoeuvre against the North Vietnamese invader," said Shackley, who went on to become CIA station chief in Vietnam from 1968 to 1973 and retired in 1979 as the number two man in the CIA's clandestine operations directorate.
In southern Laos, the U.S. strategy was "to combat Hanoi's illegal use of Laotian territory to infiltrate men and material into South Vietnam," Shackley said.

Red flags with the elephant seal of the pre-communist Lao monarchy flapped in the spring breeze as Shackley spoke beneath a white tent. He wore the "Order of A Million Elephants" decoration awarded to him in 1968 by Savang Vattana, the deposed Lao king.
Shackley, in an interview, said the secret army was made up of 40,000 troops, about 22,000 of them Hmong, also known at the time as Meo, and other ethnic minorities, lowland Lao and Thai irregulars.
He said 20,000 Hmong died in the conflict, sparing many American lives as they tied down 70,000 communist troops.
